params.title: Receivers
params.subtitle: How a superheterodyne receiver picks one station out of many, makes it strong and turns it back into sound.

onScreen: How a receiver picks one station, makes it strong and turns it back into sound
scenes.narration: Welcome to Receivers. Every radio you'll service, from a ship's radio to an aircraft radio, has a receiver inside. When it goes deaf or noisy, you're the one who has to find out why. In this lesson we'll follow a signal through the kind of receiver the exam asks about, called the superheterodyne, one stage at a time. We'll start from scratch: what any receiver has to do. Then we'll meet each stage: what it does, how it works, and what goes wrong. By the end, you'll be able to work out which unwanted frequencies can sneak into a receiver and pick the right filter width for a signal. And you'll be ready for the exam questions in this subelement.

params.title: A radio signal and its frequency
labels: A radio signal: a voltage swinging up and down
1 complete swing = 1 cycle
Cycles per second = frequency, in hertz
1000 hertz = 1 kilohertz; 1000 kilohertz = 1 megahertz

onScreen: A radio signal: a voltage swinging up and down
Cycles per second = frequency, in hertz
scenes.narration: Let's start with what a radio signal is. When a radio wave passes an antenna, it makes a tiny voltage, an electrical push, that swings up and down, over and over. One complete swing, up, down and back, is called a cycle. How many cycles happen each second is the frequency, measured in hertz: 1 hertz is 1 cycle per second. Radio frequencies are huge numbers, so we use bigger units. 1000 hertz is 1 kilohertz, and 1000 kilohertz is 1 megahertz. A signal at 151 megahertz, a number we'll meet again later, swings 151 million times every second. Every station has its own frequency, like its own address.

blocks.label: Antenna
blocks.note: Picks up every station at once

blocks.label: Select
blocks.note: Keep one frequency, reject the rest

scenes.narration: So the antenna delivers a crowd of signals, every station at once, each on its own frequency, and all of them very weak. A receiver has 3 jobs. First, select: keep the one frequency you tuned to and reject all the others. How well it does that is called selectivity. Second, amplify. An amplifier is a circuit that makes a signal bigger, and how many times bigger is its gain. A receiver needs a lot of gain, so it uses several amplifier stages in a row. Third, recover the message. The voice was added to the radio signal at the transmitter, a process called modulation, and the receiver's detector takes it back out so a speaker can play it.

onScreen: Noise floor: the receiver's own internal noise
Weakest usable signal: just above the noise floor
scenes.narration: Amplifiers have a catch: noise. Every wire and part holds electrons, the tiny charged particles that carry current, and ordinary heat makes them jiggle at random. That makes a faint hiss, even with no signal at all, and the amplifiers boost it along with everything else. This steady background of the receiver's own internal noise is its noise floor. Sensitivity is how weak a signal a receiver can still pick up. Think of a whisper in a noisy room: if it's quieter than the chatter, no one hears it. Likewise, a receiver cannot detect signals weaker than its own internal noise. So for the exam, the limiting condition for sensitivity is the noise floor of the receiver.

marks.label: Minimum discernible signal
marks.note: The weakest you can make out

marks.label: Largest tolerable signal
marks.note: The strongest it takes without overload

onScreen: Dynamic range: the ratio between them
scenes.narration: The noise floor sets the bottom limit. Just above it is the minimum discernible signal, the weakest signal you can make out. At the top is the largest tolerable input signal, the strongest the receiver can take without overload. The ratio between the largest tolerable receiver input signal and the minimum discernible signal is called dynamic range. Ratio means how many times stronger one is than the other. Like your ears, which hear a whisper and take a shout, a receiver with a wide dynamic range handles both. But go past the top, with a very strong signal from a transmitter close by, and the stages are pushed harder than they were built for. They overload, and the sound distorts.

params.title: The superheterodyne idea
items: Selecting one station needs a very sharp filter
A sharp filter is hard to retune across a whole band
The trick: shift every station to one fixed frequency
IF: intermediate frequency, between radio and audio
Fixed IF filters and amplifiers: sharp and strong

onScreen: Hard to retune across a band
Shift every station to one frequency
scenes.narration: Back to those 3 jobs. How does one receiver do them for any station you tune? Selecting takes a filter: a circuit that passes some frequencies and blocks others. To pick out one station among many, the filter must be very sharp, and a filter that sharp is very hard to retune across a whole band. The superheterodyne gets around this with a trick. Instead of moving the filter to the station, it moves the station to the filter. Whatever you tune is shifted to one fixed frequency, called the IF, or intermediate frequency: intermediate because it sits between the radio frequency and the audio you hear. Filters and amplifiers built for that one frequency can be sharp and strong.

blocks.label: Mixer
blocks.note: Shifts it to one fixed frequency

onScreen: Mixer: shifts it to one fixed frequency
Local oscillator, retuned by the dial
IF: intermediate frequency, fixed filters and amplifiers
scenes.narration: Here's how the shift is done. The station you tune goes into a stage called the mixer, which shifts it to the IF. Heterodyne is an old word for mixing 2 frequencies, and that's where the superheterodyne gets its name. To mix, the mixer needs a second signal, and the receiver makes its own in the local oscillator, or LO. An oscillator is a circuit that generates a steady signal of its own; we'll see how one works later. Turning the tuning dial really retunes the LO. It always stays the same distance from the station you want, so that station always lands on the IF, ready for the fixed IF filters and amplifiers.

blocks.label: Mixer · block 1
blocks.note: Shifts the signal to the IF

onScreen: IF amplifiers: most of the gain
AGC, block 4, and the audio amplifier
scenes.narration: Now the whole receiver, as the exam draws it in pool Figure 3F15, with 4 of its blocks numbered. First comes the RF, or radio frequency, amplifier, which gives the signal a small lift. Next, the mixer, block 1, shifts the signal to the IF. The IF amplifiers provide most of the receiver's gain. The detector, block 3, recovers the audio. Below, the local oscillator, block 2, feeds the mixer. Block 4 is the AGC, or automatic gain control: it turns the IF gain down when the signal is strong, so loud and weak stations sound alike. Last, the audio amplifier drives the speaker. The stages from the antenna up to the mixer are called the front end.

params.title: Noise figure: the noise made inside
items: Every stage adds a little noise of its own
Noise figure: noise generated in the front end and succeeding stages
Noise arriving from the antenna is not part of it
Lower noise figure: a quieter receiver

onScreen: Noise figure: noise made in the front end and later stages
Antenna noise is not part of it
scenes.narration: Back to noise, because every stage in that chain adds a little of its own. The exam has a name for how much a receiver adds. The noise figure of a receiver is the level of noise generated in the front end and succeeding stages of the receiver. Succeeding just means the stages that follow. Some noise also arrives from the antenna, from lightning, engines or space, but that comes in with the signal, so it's not part of the noise figure. The noise figure measures only the receiver's own contribution, so the lower it is, the quieter the receiver. And it isn't selectivity, the rejecting of nearby signals: that's a different answer.

params.title: Why the first stage matters most

blocks.label: Antenna
blocks.note: Outside noise: not in the noise figure

blocks.label: RF amplifier
blocks.note: Its noise is amplified by every later stage

blocks.label: Mixer
blocks.note: Adds noise after the RF gain

onScreen: Antenna noise: not part of the noise figure
RF stage: sets the noise figure
scenes.narration: Follow the signal in from the antenna. Which stage's noise matters most? The first. Picture a line of people passing a message along, each repeating it louder: a mumble from the first gets amplified by everyone after. In the same way, noise made in the RF stage, our RF amplifier, is amplified by every stage after it. Noise added later is amplified less, so it counts for less. That's why the RF stage primarily establishes a receiver's noise figure. The audio stage, the IF strip, meaning the chain of IF amplifiers, and the local oscillator are traps.

params.title: Desensitizing or intermodulation?
rows: A strong signal on a nearby frequency

onScreen: Caused by a strong signal on a nearby frequency
Caused by 2 or more strong signals mixing
scenes.narration: Strong signals, at the top of the dynamic range, cause trouble too. Suppose a powerful transmitter sits on the adjacent channel, next to yours. It can overload the front end, or drive the AGC to turn the gain right down. Either way, your weak station fades. That reduction in receiver sensitivity because of a strong signal on a nearby frequency is called desensitizing. The exam also words it as a reduction in sensitivity caused by unwanted high-level adjacent channel signals: still desensitizing. Overloading is the cause, not the name. Don't confuse it with intermodulation, when 2 or more strong signals mix into spurious signals, false signals where nothing was sent. Desensitizing takes signals away; intermodulation adds fake ones.

params.title: The tuned circuit
labels: Front end: the first job is selectivity
Tuned circuit: a coil joined to a capacitor
Energy swings between them: strongest at one frequency
Change a part, and it tunes to a new frequency

scenes.narration: We've seen what limits a receiver: noise at the bottom, strong signals at the top. Both battles are fought in the front end, so let's zoom in on it, starting at the antenna. The first job is selectivity, and the front end gets it from a tuned circuit. That's a coil of wire joined to a capacitor, which is 2 metal plates with a thin gap that store electric charge. Energy swings back and forth between them. Like a swing that goes highest when pushed in time with its own rhythm, a tuned circuit responds strongly to one frequency and weakly to others. Change either part, and it tunes to a new frequency.

blocks.label: Preselector
blocks.note: Tuned circuit: passes only your band

onScreen: Preselector: a tuned circuit ahead of the RF amplifier
Extra amplifier stages add gain, not selectivity
scenes.narration: Placed ahead of the RF amplifier and mixer, a tuned circuit is called a preselector, because it selects first. It passes the band you've tuned to and weakens strong signals on other frequencies before they reach the stages behind it. So selectivity in the front-end circuitry is achieved by a preselector. An additional RF or IF amplifier stage adds gain, not selectivity: it makes everything bigger, wanted and unwanted alike. And an audio filter comes far too late, after the signal has already been through the front end.

params.title: What the RF amplifier is for
items: Most of the gain comes from the IF stages, not the RF amplifier
Primary purpose: improve the receiver's noise figure
Low noise amplifier: most useful in a VHF receiver's front end RF stage
The first stage sets the noise figure of the whole receiver

onScreen: RF amplifier: improves the noise figure
Low noise amplifier: front end RF stage
First stage sets the noise figure
scenes.narration: After the preselector comes the RF amplifier. You might think its job is gain, but mainly it isn't. Most of the receiver's gain comes from the IF stages. The primary purpose of an RF amplifier in a receiver is to improve the receiver's noise figure. It gives the weak signal a clean lift before the noisier stages behind it add their hiss. That's why a low noise amplifier is most advantageous in the front end RF stage of a VHF, or very high frequency, receiver. Remember, the first stage sets the noise figure of the whole receiver. A low noise amplifier in the IF stage, the audio stage or the power supply would gain you little.

marks.label: Weak signal after RF gain
marks.note: Lifted just above the mixer noise

onScreen: Enough gain for weak signals to overcome it
scenes.narration: So how much gain should the RF amplifier have? The mixer behind it makes noise of its own. The RF amplifier needs sufficient gain to allow weak signals to overcome the noise generated in the first mixer stage. That's just enough to lift them clear, not as much gain as possible. Once the weak signal is clear of the mixer noise, more gain raises the signal and the RF amplifier's own noise together, so you hear no better. But it does boost every strong signal nearby. Too much gain in a VHF receiver front end causes susceptibility to intermodulation interference from nearby transmitters. Their amplified signals overload the mixer and mix with each other, creating false signals on your channel.

params.title: Transistors and the GaAsFET
items: Transistor: a small signal controls a larger current
FET: field-effect transistor
GaAsFET: a FET made of gallium arsenide
Fast electrons: high gain, very little added noise

onScreen: Transistor: a small signal controls a larger current
scenes.narration: What part makes a good low noise RF amplifier? Amplifiers are built around transistors. A transistor is a tiny electronic part, usually made of silicon, in which a small signal controls a larger current. The larger current copies the small signal, only bigger. That's where an amplifier's gain comes from. One family is the FET, the field-effect transistor. A FET made from gallium arsenide instead of silicon is called a GaAsFET. Electrons move very quickly through gallium arsenide, so a GaAsFET amplifies VHF signals well while adding very little noise of its own.

params.title: The GaAsFET preamplifier
items: Preamplifier: the first amplifier in the chain
GaAsFET preamplifier: high gain and a low noise floor
Trap: high gain with a high noise floor
Front end: tune first, then clean, modest gain

onScreen: High gain and a low noise floor
Tune first, then clean, modest gain
scenes.narration: That makes the GaAsFET a natural choice for the preamplifier, the very first amplifier in the chain, ahead of everything else. For the exam, the advantage of a GaAsFET preamplifier in a modern VHF receiver is high gain and a low noise floor. Watch the wording: high gain with a high noise floor is a trap. So are the answers about selectivity, which comes from the preselector, not the amplifier. Here's the whole front end in one line: a preselector tunes first. Then a low noise RF amplifier adds just enough clean gain to lift weak signals above the mixer's noise.

blocks.label: Output
blocks.note: A steady signal of its own

onScreen: Output: a signal of its own
scenes.narration: We've followed the signal through the front end. But the mixer can't work alone: it needs that second signal from the local oscillator. So how does a circuit make a signal of its own, with no input? You've heard it happen by accident: hold a microphone near its loudspeaker and you get a howl, as the sound goes round and round, louder each time. An oscillator does that on purpose. Some of an amplifier's output is fed back to its input in step, rising when the input rises, so it adds to it. That's called positive feedback. Round and round it goes, and the circuit keeps itself going.

params.title: Will it oscillate?
rows: Gain less than 1 around the loop

scenes.narration: How much feedback does it take? Each trip around the loop loses a little, so the feedback must make up for those losses. For the exam, to oscillate, a circuit must have sufficient positive feedback. With a gain of less than 1 around the loop, the signal shrinks each lap and dies away. Negative feedback is fed back opposite to the input, so it cancels instead of adding. Neutralization is used in amplifiers that must not oscillate: it cancels the feedback that leaks from output to input inside the transistor. So negative feedback and neutralization both suppress oscillation, which makes them trap answers.

What sets an oscillator's frequency? Usually a tuned circuit, the coil and capacitor of the preselector: it naturally oscillates at its own frequency, like the swing, and the feedback keeps it going. The 3 major oscillator circuits found in radio equipment differ in how they take their feedback. The Colpitts uses a capacitive divider: 2 capacitors connected one after the other, with the feedback taken from the point between them. The Hartley uses a tapped coil, a coil with a connection partway along it. And the Pierce is crystal-controlled: a thin slice of quartz that vibrates at one very exact frequency, like a tuning fork. So: Colpitts, Hartley and Pierce. Any list with Taft in it is a trap.

params.title: The VFO: why Colpitts
items: VFO: variable frequency oscillator, tuned by the dial
Colpitts: the circuit commonly used in a VFO
Why: it is stable
Pierce: crystal-controlled, essentially fixed in frequency

onScreen: Colpitts: commonly used in a VFO
scenes.narration: Which of these suits a local oscillator you tune with a dial? Such an oscillator is a VFO, a variable frequency oscillator, and the circuit commonly used in a VFO is the Colpitts. Why? Because it is stable: its frequency stays put once you set it. Its capacitive divider uses fairly large capacitors, and they swamp the tiny, drifting capacitor-like effects inside the transistor, so warming up changes the frequency very little. The Pierce is out, because a crystal oscillator is essentially fixed in frequency; you can't tune it across a band. And one trap answer talks about the crystal's stability, but a VFO has no crystal at all.

Many modern radios make their local oscillator signal a different way, with a frequency synthesizer. That's a circuit that can produce any frequency you select, all locked to one very stable reference. It starts with that reference standard, a very stable oscillator, usually crystal-controlled. Next comes a phase detector, which compares 2 signals. Phase means where a wave is in its cycle, so it can tell whether 2 signals keep step. Its output, a correction voltage, steers the VCO, the voltage-controlled oscillator, whose frequency follows that voltage. The VCO is the oscillator that actually makes the output: the selected frequency, sent on to the mixer.

onScreen: Divider: divides by a whole number
Phase detector: compares with the reference
scenes.narration: What does the phase detector compare? Follow the loop from the VCO, which puts out the selected frequency. A sample goes back through a divider, which divides the VCO frequency by a whole number. Change that number, and the VCO must move to match: that's how you pick a new channel. The divided signal reaches the phase detector, and any difference from the reference becomes the correction voltage that pulls the VCO onto frequency. The whole loop is a PLL, a phase-locked loop: it locks the VCO in step with the reference standard. For the exam, the oscillator stage in a frequency synthesizer is the VCO; the divider, phase detector and reference standard are the loop's other blocks.

callouts.label: Block 1: the mixer, right after the RF amplifier
Block 2: the circle feeding the mixer from below
Block 2 is the symbol for the local oscillator
Blocks 3 and 4: the detector and the AGC
Oscillators: positive feedback, a Colpitts VFO, a synthesizer's VCO

onScreen: Block 2 feeds the mixer from below
scenes.narration: However the local oscillator is built, the exam's diagram shows it the same way. In pool Figure 3F15, block 1, the circle right after the RF amplifier, is the mixer. Block 2 is the circle feeding the mixer from below. Block 2 is the symbol for the local oscillator: it supplies the second signal the mixer needs. Block 3 is the detector and block 4 the AGC, so those are traps. So for oscillators: positive feedback keeps them going, the Colpitts makes a stable VFO, and a synthesizer's oscillator is the VCO. Next, let's see what happens when the 2 signals meet in the mixer.

params.title: Mixing: sum and difference
items: Mixer: combines 2 signals
Like 2 guitar strings beating at their difference
Out come the sum and the difference frequencies

onScreen: Guitar strings beat at their difference
scenes.narration: In the mixer, the incoming signal and the local oscillator's signal meet. What comes out? You may have heard something like it: 2 guitar strings slightly out of tune make a slow, pulsing beat at the difference between their pitches. A mixer does this electrically, and it makes the sum as well as the difference. So the mixing process in a radio receiver is the combination of 2 signals to produce sum and difference frequencies. Answers about removing noise by phase comparison, or distortion from the aurora, describe something else.

blocks.label: Mixer output
blocks.note: Originals, plus their sum and difference

onScreen: IF filter keeps the difference: 455 kHz
scenes.narration: Let's try real numbers. A 14.255 megahertz signal comes into the mixer, and the local oscillator feeds it 13.8 megahertz. The principal frequencies at the mixer's output are the original frequencies, plus their sum and their difference: not square roots, and not 2 or 4 times the input. Here the difference is 14.255 minus 13.8, which is 0.455 megahertz, or 455 kilohertz. Each frequency that comes out is called a product. The IF filter after the mixer then selects the wanted product, usually the difference, and throws the rest away.

params.title: Overdriving the mixer
items: A mixer should make just the sum and difference
Excessive signal energy overdrives it
Result: spurious mixer products are generated
Not automatic limiting, mixer blanking or drift

scenes.narration: A mixer only behaves well within limits. What if far too strong a signal reaches it? Excessive amounts of signal energy overdriving the mixer circuit generate spurious mixer products. Spurious means false. Driven too hard, the mixer starts making extra frequencies, multiples of its inputs and mixtures of those, beyond the intended sum and difference. Some fall in the IF and sound like signals that were never sent. It's the same family of trouble as the intermodulation we met at the front end. The trap answers, automatic limiting, mixer blanking, or the mixer drifting, don't describe it.

params.title: The image: the same distance on the other side

marks.label: Signal: 151.000 MHz
marks.note: 11 MHz above the LO: mixes to the IF

marks.label: Image: 129.000 MHz
marks.note: 11 MHz below the LO: the same IF

onScreen: Signal 151.000 MHz, 11 MHz above the LO
Image 129.000 MHz, 11 MHz below the LO
scenes.narration: Even a well-behaved mixer has a weak spot: the image frequency. Here's the exam's example. The station you want is at 151 megahertz, and the LO is at 140 megahertz. Their difference is 11 megahertz, so the IF is 11 megahertz. But the mixer only cares about the distance from the LO, not which side it's on. A signal at 129 megahertz sits 11 megahertz below the LO, so its difference from the LO is also 11 megahertz. It drops into the IF just as neatly as the wanted station. That unwanted second frequency is called the image. When the LO is below the signal, the image lies the same IF distance below the LO.

params.title: Image frequency: LO below the signal

onScreen: Signal 151.000 MHz, IF 11.000 MHz, LO 140.000 MHz
scenes.narration: Let's turn that into a formula. f sub image is the image frequency, f sub LO the local oscillator frequency, and IF the intermediate frequency. When the LO is below the signal, f sub image equals f sub LO minus IF. Step 1: the givens. The normal channel is 151.000 megahertz, the IF 11.000 megahertz, and the LO 140.000 megahertz, below the channel, so the formula fits. Step 2: 140 minus 11 is 129 megahertz. Step 3: check. The signal is one IF above the LO and the image one IF below, so they're 2 IFs apart: 151 minus 2 times 11 is also 129. The image frequency is 129.000 megahertz. Got 162.000? That's the IF added to the channel.

blocks.label: RF stage
blocks.note: Tuned to 151.000 MHz: rejects the image

blocks.label: IF: 11.000 MHz
blocks.note: An image here can't be separated

onScreen: RF stage tuned to 151.000 MHz rejects it
Past the mixer, the image can't be separated
scenes.narration: Where should the image be stopped? Follow it in from the antenna. First it meets the RF stage, with its tuned preselector and RF amplifier, set to pass 151 megahertz but not 129. If the image gets past them, it reaches the mixer, and the mixer converts it to exactly the same IF as the desired signal. From then on the 2 are on one frequency, and no IF filter can pull them apart. That's why the image frequency is normally rejected in the RF stage, before the mixer. The IF, the LO and the detector are the wrong answers: by then, it's too late.

params.title: Second example: a 455 kHz IF
steps: Signal 14.255 MHz, VFO 13.8 MHz, IF 455 kHz
455 kHz = 0.455 MHz, so the units match

onScreen: Signal 14.255 MHz, VFO 13.8 MHz, IF 455 kHz
scenes.narration: Now the second exam example. A receiver mixes a 13.8 megahertz VFO with a 14.255 megahertz receive signal to produce a 455 kilohertz IF. Here the VFO is the local oscillator. The VFO is below the signal, so f sub image equals f sub VFO minus IF. Write the IF as 0.455 megahertz, so the units match. 13.8 minus 0.455 is 13.345 megahertz. Does that make sense? The wanted signal is 0.455 megahertz above the VFO, and 13.345 is the same distance below. That means a 13.345 megahertz signal also mixes down to 455 kilohertz: it produces an image response. So for mixers: sum and difference come out, and an image waits on the far side of the LO.

params.title: Sidebands: a signal takes up a band
labels: Carrier: the station's own frequency
Sidebands: the voice, above and below the carrier
Each sideband about 5 kHz wide
Bandwidth: 2 × 5 = 10 kHz

scenes.narration: Next stop: the IF amplifiers and their filters. To size a filter, we need to know how wide a signal is. A station isn't a single frequency. In the middle sits its steady radio signal, the carrier. In AM, amplitude modulation, the voice makes the carrier's strength, its amplitude, rise and fall. That's mixing again: the voice and the carrier combine into sums and differences, new frequencies just above and below the carrier, called sidebands. Each sideband is as wide as the highest audio it carries. For voice up to about 5 kilohertz, that's 5 kilohertz on each side, so the whole signal occupies 2 times 5, or 10 kilohertz: its bandwidth. With 2 sidebands, it's double-sideband AM.

marks.label: Too-wide passband edge
marks.note: Lets undesired signals reach the audio stage

onScreen: IF passband slightly wider than the signal
Too wide: undesired signals reach the audio
scenes.narration: How wide should the IF filter be? Picture a highway: every station needs a lane wide enough for it. The filter's passband, the range of frequencies it lets through, should be slightly greater than the received-signal bandwidth. Slightly wider, so all the sidebands pass and none of the voice is cut off. Not much wider, so extra noise and neighboring lanes stay out. Half the signal's width would chop the voice; 2 or 4 times would let in the neighbors. If the filter bandwidth in the IF section is too wide, undesired signals will reach the audio stage. The exam calls the width the IF passes its selectivity. So for double-sideband AM, 10 kilohertz of IF selectivity is optimum.

params.title: Single sideband: 2.4 kHz
labels: Carrier removed
One sideband kept, the other removed
Speech: about 300 to 2700 Hz
IF selectivity: 2.4 kHz

scenes.narration: Look again at that AM signal. Both sidebands carry the same voice, and the carrier carries no voice at all. SSB, single sideband, removes the carrier and one sideband, and sends just the other. That saves power and takes far less room. Speech for communication is trimmed to roughly 300 to 2700 hertz, which is still easy to understand, and that range is about 2.4 kilohertz wide. That's why a receiver selectivity of 2.4 kilohertz in the IF circuitry is optimum for SSB voice: it fits one sideband of speech. Double-sideband AM needs 10 kilohertz, and Morse code needs far less.

params.title: Wideband FM phone: 15 kHz
labels: FM: the voice swings the carrier's frequency
Deviation: ±5 kHz
Plus sidebands beyond the swing
IF selectivity: about 15 kHz

onScreen: FM: the voice swings the frequency
scenes.narration: FM, frequency modulation, works differently. Instead of changing the carrier's strength, the voice swings its frequency a little above and below the center, louder sounds swinging it farther. How far it swings is called the deviation. A voice FM signal with plus or minus 5 kilohertz deviation swings across 10 kilohertz. The swinging itself happens thousands of times a second, and that throws off sidebands a little beyond the swings, so altogether the signal occupies roughly 15 kilohertz. So the selectivity desirable in the IF circuitry of a wideband FM phone receiver is 15 kilohertz. Phone just means voice. Filters of 1, 2.4 or 4.2 kilohertz would chop off much of the FM signal.

Here are the 3 exam numbers side by side. The rule behind all of them is the same: the IF should be just a little wider than the signal. Wideband FM phone needs 15 kilohertz. Double-sideband AM needs 10 kilohertz, 2 sidebands of 5 kilohertz each. SSB voice needs 2.4 kilohertz, one sideband of speech. On the exam, watch for the swaps: 2.4 kilohertz offered for FM, or SSB voice offered for 10 kilohertz.

params.title: SAW IF filters
items: SAW: surface acoustic wave, used as a receiver IF filter
A tiny piezoelectric chip with patterned electrodes
So it can be used in micro-miniature electronic circuits

onScreen: SAW: surface acoustic wave IF filter
scenes.narration: How do you build a sharp IF filter that's also tiny? One answer is the SAW, or surface acoustic wave, filter. It's a small chip of piezoelectric material, a crystal that flexes when a voltage is applied, and makes a voltage when it flexes. Metal electrodes patterned on the chip turn the electrical signal into a tiny sound wave rippling across its surface, and other electrodes turn it back. The pattern decides which frequencies get through. Because it's so small, a receiver SAW IF filter can be used in micro-miniature electronic circuits. A high power transmitter cavity, by contrast, is large. The takeaway for the IF: make the filter fit the signal.

onScreen: First IF amplifier: selectivity (crystal, ceramic or mechanical filter)
scenes.narration: So the IF needs a sharp filter and plenty of gain. In practice it has several amplifier stages, and the first and final ones have different jobs. The mixer feeds the first IF amplifier stage. Its primary purpose is selectivity. That's where the sharp filter sits: a crystal, ceramic or mechanical filter, all parts that vibrate readily only at the frequencies to be passed. Noise figure isn't its job; that was settled back at the RF stage. By the final IF amplifier stage, the unwanted signals are already gone, so its primary purpose is gain. It raises the signal to the strong level the detector and the AGC need to work.

params.title: Choosing an intermediate frequency
items: Weigh image rejection and selectivity
The image sits 2 IFs away from the signal
Higher IF: image farther away, easier to reject
Lower IF: narrow selectivity is easier

scenes.narration: Which frequency should a designer pick for the IF, then? For the exam, the factors to consider are image rejection and selectivity, and they pull in opposite directions. Cross-modulation, noise figure and interference to other services are the traps. Remember that the image sits 2 IFs away from the wanted signal: 151 and 129 megahertz are 2 times 11 apart. A higher IF puts the image farther away, so the preselector rejects it easily. A lower IF makes narrow selectivity easier, because a filter's width tends to grow with its center frequency: at a low frequency, the same parts make a narrower filter. Every IF choice trades one against the other.

We keep saying filter, so let's look at filters properly. A filter lets some frequencies through and stops others, like a sieve sorting by size. The range of frequencies it passes is its passband. The frequency where it starts stopping them is its cut-off frequency. How does it choose? Most filters are built from coils and capacitors. A coil resists changes in current, so it passes low frequencies easily and resists high ones, which change fastest. A capacitor does the reverse: it blocks slow changes and passes fast ones. Arranged the right way, they let the passband through, while signals beyond the cut-off are weakened, or attenuated.

Filters are named for what they pass. A low-pass filter passes frequencies below its cut-off, and stops those above. A high-pass filter does the opposite: it passes those above its cut-off. A band-pass filter passes a band between 2 cut-offs, which is exactly what an IF filter is. So the 3 general groupings of filters are high-pass, low-pass and band-pass. Hartley, Colpitts and Pierce are oscillators, not filters, and inductive, capacitive and resistive are kinds of parts, so both answers are traps. One more type is worth knowing: the band-stop filter, the opposite of band-pass. It stops one band in the middle and passes the rest.

callouts.label: Up the side: amplitude; along the bottom: frequency
Curve A: low-pass, passes the low frequencies
Curve B: band-pass, passes a band in the middle
Curve C: high-pass, passes the high frequencies
Curve D: band-stop, stops a band in the middle

scenes.narration: Those types are exactly what the exam shows in pool Figure 3F16. Each graph plots amplitude, how strong the output is, up the side, against frequency along the bottom, low to high, left to right. Curve A starts high, then drops: it passes the lows and stops the highs, so curve A is a low pass curve. Curve B is low at both ends and high in the middle: band-pass. Curve C is the reverse of A: high-pass. And curve D is the opposite of B: it dips in the middle, stopping one band, so curve D is a band stop curve. For the exam: A is low pass, D is band stop.

params.title: The SSB crystal filter
items: Crystal band-pass filter for single-sideband phone: 2.1 kHz wide
Wide enough for intelligible speech
Narrow enough to reject the opposite sideband
Not to be confused with 2.4 kHz, the SSB voice IF selectivity

scenes.narration: Receivers lean hardest on band-pass filters, and ones made from quartz crystals are sharp enough to separate one sideband from the other. A good crystal band-pass filter for a single-sideband phone is 2.1 kilohertz wide. That's wide enough for intelligible speech, speech you can understand, while still rejecting the opposite sideband sitting right next to it. 500 hertz suits Morse code, and 15 kilohertz suits FM. The exam asks about 2 separate numbers here, so keep them apart: 2.1 kilohertz for this crystal filter, and 2.4 kilohertz for the IF selectivity of SSB voice. Both are about one sideband of speech wide; the exam simply uses one number for each question.

params.title: Butterworth: maximally flat
items: Rolloff: how quickly the output falls beyond cut-off
Ripple: waviness across the passband
Butterworth: maximally flat response over its passband
Uses both inductors and capacitors, not one kind alone

scenes.narration: Filters also differ in the shape of their response, meaning how strongly they pass each frequency. First, 2 new words. Rolloff is how quickly a filter's output falls beyond the cut-off frequency: steep is like a cliff edge, gradual like a gentle hill. Ripple is a little up-and-down waviness across the passband. A Butterworth filter has a maximally flat response over its passband: no ripple at all, every frequency inside passed equally, then a smooth fall after the cut-off. It's built with both inductors, the proper name for coils, and capacitors. Coils and capacitors do opposite jobs, as we saw, and the filter needs both to shape its response, so answers saying it needs only one kind are wrong.

onScreen: Chebyshev: ripple in the passband, steeper rolloff
scenes.narration: The Butterworth's rival, the Chebyshev filter, makes a trade. A Chebyshev filter is distinguished by allowing ripple in its passband. In exchange it gets a steeper rolloff, cutting off more sharply than a Butterworth built from the same number of parts. The maximally flat passband belongs to the Butterworth, which gives up some of that steepness. So if a question mentions ripple in the passband, think Chebyshev. If it says maximally flat, think Butterworth. One more answer offered here describes the constant-k filter, which we'll meet next.

params.title: The constant-k filter
items: Series parts: in line with the signal path
Shunt parts: across from the line to ground
Impedance: opposition to AC, changes with frequency
Constant-k: series × shunt impedance = a constant
High attenuation far from the passband; gradual near cut-off

onScreen: High attenuation far from the passband, gradual near cut-off
scenes.narration: The next pair of filters depends on how the parts are arranged. In a ladder filter, drawn like the rungs of a ladder, some parts are in series: in line with the signal path. Others are in shunt: connected across from the signal line to ground, the circuit's common return. Each part's impedance is its opposition to AC, alternating current. For coils and capacitors, impedance changes with frequency. In a constant-k filter, multiply the series- and shunt-element impedances together, and that product stays constant at all frequencies: k is that constant. Its advantage is high attenuation, strong weakening, of signals at frequencies far removed from the passband. Its weakness is a gradual rolloff close to the cut-off.

params.title: When to choose an m-derived filter

marks.label: Unwanted frequency
marks.note: Too close to cut-off for a constant-k filter

onScreen: Unwanted frequency too close to cut-off for constant-k
scenes.narration: That weakness is where the m-derived filter comes in. Here's a filter's passband, the frequencies it lets through. Here's its cut-off frequency, where attenuation begins. Now suppose an unwanted signal sits just beyond the cut-off. A constant-k filter is still rolling off gently there, so it can't weaken that signal enough. For the exam, an m-derived filter is more desirable than a constant-k filter when you need more attenuation at a certain frequency that is too close to the cut-off frequency for a constant-k filter. It adds a trap, a tuned circuit set to that exact frequency, which carves a deep notch right where it's needed. A maximally flat response, fewer parts or high power aren't the reason.

params.title: Constant-k, m-derived and Butterworth
rows: Constant product of series and shunt impedances
High attenuation far from the passband
A trap added to the filter

onScreen: Constant-k: constant series and shunt impedance product
Constant-k: high attenuation far from the passband
Butterworth: maximally flat, inductors and capacitors
scenes.narration: Let's sort the 3 filter families, because the exam swaps their descriptions around. A constant-k filter is the one described by a constant product of its series- and shunt-element impedances, and its advantage is high attenuation far from the passband. An m-derived filter is a filter that uses a trap to attenuate undesired frequencies too near cut-off for a constant-k filter. The constant product describes the constant-k filter, not the m-derived one, and m-derived has nothing to do with a schematic shaped like the letter M. A Butterworth has the maximally flat passband, built from inductors and capacitors together.

params.title: Designing an op-amp audio filter
items: Op-amp: a complete amplifier on one chip
Its behavior is set by the parts around it
Select the bandpass characteristics: center frequency, bandwidth, cut-off points
Traps: current gain, temperature coefficient, output-offset overshoot

onScreen: Op-amp: an amplifier on a chip
Set by the parts around it
Traps: current gain, temperature coefficient, offset overshoot
scenes.narration: Filters don't have to be made of coils. At audio frequencies, a filter is often built around an op-amp, an operational amplifier: a complete amplifier on one small chip. Its behavior is set by a few resistors, parts that oppose current, and capacitors around it. Say you want an audio filter that keeps speech and drops a whistle. When designing an audio filter using an op-amp, the parameter you must select is its bandpass characteristics: the center frequency, the bandwidth and the cut-off points. Once those are chosen, the part values follow. Current gain, temperature coefficient and output-offset overshoot are traps. That wraps up filters: choose the shape and the width to fit the job.

blocks.label: Transmitter
blocks.note: Modulation: puts the voice on the carrier

blocks.label: Receiver detector
blocks.note: Detection: takes the voice back off

scenes.narration: The signal has been filtered and amplified. Now it reaches the detector, block 3 in Figure 3F15. At the transmitter, modulation put the voice onto the carrier, and the signal crossed the radio path to us. Detection in a radio receiver is the reverse: the recovery of intelligence from the modulated RF signal. Intelligence here just means the information carried, whether that's voice, Morse code or data. So modulation happens at the transmitter, and detection is the opposite process, done at the receiver. Masking out the intelligence, or mixing noise with the signal, are trap answers. Different kinds of modulation need different detectors, and there are 3 to know.

params.title: Inside the diode detector
labels: An AM signal: an RF carrier inside its audio envelope
The envelope: the shape of the sound
Rectification keeps one polarity
Filtering removes the RF, leaving the audio envelope

onScreen: AM signal with its audio envelope
Envelope: the shape of the sound
scenes.narration: First, the diode detector, used for AM. A diode is a part that lets current flow in one direction only, like a one-way valve. An AM signal arrives: a fast radio frequency carrier whose peaks rise and fall with the audio. The line tracing those peaks is called the envelope, and it has the shape of the sound. The diode lets through only one polarity, the top half of each swing; that's rectification. Why? Left whole, the top and bottom halves would average out to nothing. Then a filter smooths away the fast RF wiggles. What's left is the audio envelope, the intelligence we wanted. So detection in a radio diode detector is rectification and filtering of RF.

SSB is trickier. Its carrier was removed at the transmitter, and a diode detector needs that carrier to work. The same goes for CW, continuous wave: Morse code sent by switching a carrier on and off. Through a diode detector it gives no tone, only clicks. So these signals go to a product detector, which uses a mixing process with a locally generated carrier. The receiver makes its own carrier with an oscillator, replacing the one SSB suppressed, and mixes it with the signal. The difference product that comes out is the audio: a voice for SSB, or a tone for CW. It isn't the mixer's local oscillator; it only borrows the mixing idea.

params.title: The frequency discriminator
labels: FM: steady strength, the voice is in the frequency swings
Discriminator: frequency changes become voltage changes
Output voltage rises and falls with the swings: the voice
A frequency discriminator detects FM phone signals

onScreen: FM: the voice is in the frequency swings
scenes.narration: FM needs a third kind of detector. An FM signal's strength stays steady; the voice is in the frequency swings. So the detector must turn changes in frequency into changes in voltage. That circuit is the frequency discriminator. As the frequency swings one way, its output voltage rises, and as it swings the other way, the voltage falls, tracing out the voice. Despite its name, it doesn't sort out 2 closely spaced signals. A frequency discriminator is a circuit for detecting FM signals, and it's the circuit used to detect FM phone signals.

params.title: Three detectors
rows: Mixes in a locally generated carrier

scenes.narration: That makes 3 signals, with a detector to match each. A diode detector handles AM: it rectifies and filters the RF. A product detector handles SSB and CW: it mixes in a locally generated carrier. The balanced modulator, a transmitter circuit used in making SSB, also belongs to the SSB world. So on an FM question, both the product detector and the balanced modulator are traps. FM, including FM phone, goes to the frequency discriminator, which turns frequency swings into voltage.

params.title: Conventional squelch: it runs on noise

onScreen: No carrier: strong noise, audio muted
Carrier arrives: noise quiets, squelch opens
Squelch works on the presence of noise
scenes.narration: The voice is back. Before it reaches the speaker, a few more circuits decide whether you hear it at all, and how clean it sounds. First, squelch. On an FM channel with no one talking, the detector puts out loud, rushing noise. Squelch is the circuit that keeps the speaker quiet until there's something to hear. A conventional squelch circuit functions on the presence of noise: it listens to the noise at the detector's output. With no carrier, the noise is strong, and the squelch mutes the audio. When a station's carrier arrives, it quiets the noise, and the squelch opens. So what causes a squelch circuit to function is the presence of noise, not its absence.

params.title: Three kinds of squelch
rows: No carrier: noise mutes the audio

scenes.narration: Plain squelch opens for any carrier. On a busy channel shared by many users, you may only want to hear your own group. CTCSS, the Continuous Tone-Coded Squelch System, adds a low tone to the transmitted audio, roughly 67 to 254 hertz. It's called sub-audible because it sits below the voice and is filtered out before you'd hear it. The receiver's squelch opens only when that specific tone is present. So a CTCSS squelch works on tones. A Digital Coded Squelch, or DCS, does the same job with digital codes, sent continuously beneath the voice. So: conventional squelch works on noise, CTCSS on tones, and DCS on digital codes.

params.title: Where the CTCSS tone is removed

blocks.label: IF amplifiers
blocks.note: Tone hidden in the FM signal

blocks.label: Frequency discriminator
blocks.note: Demodulates the FM: the tone appears

scenes.narration: Where does the receiver remove that CTCSS tone, so you don't hear it? Follow the signal. In the IF, the tone is still hidden inside the FM signal, as part of its frequency swings. It only exists as a tone once the frequency discriminator has demodulated the FM, so it can't be removed any earlier. In a CTCSS controlled FM receiver, the tone is filtered out after the discriminator but before the audio section. A filter there passes the voice and stops the low tone, while the squelch circuit still listens for it. Answers placing it before the mixer, the IF or the discriminator are too early.

blocks.label: Receiver de-emphasis
blocks.note: Cuts the highs by the same amount

scenes.narration: Another trick shapes the audio itself. Noise picked up along the way, especially in FM, sounds mostly like hiss, and hiss lives in the high audio frequencies. So at the transmitter, pre-emphasis boosts the high audio frequencies before sending. Along the radio path, noise adds its hiss. At the receiver, de-emphasis cuts the highs by the same amount the transmitter boosted them. The voice comes out with its natural balance, which we call flat audio, and the hiss, which was never boosted, is cut along with the highs. So receiver de-emphasis, coupled with transmitter pre-emphasis, gives flat audio and noise reduction. The trap answer stops at flat audio alone.

Today, much of this audio work is done with DSP, digital signal processing: handling the signal as numbers inside a small computer chip. An analog signal, a smoothly varying voltage, comes in. The DSP circuit samples it in an analog-to-digital converter. Sampling means measuring the voltage many thousands of times a second and writing each measurement down as a number. The chip records and processes those numbers, for filtering or noise reduction, then converts them back to an analog signal in a digital-to-analog converter, ready for the speaker. So the circuit that samples analog signals, records and processes them as numbers, then converts them back is the digital signal processing circuit.

params.title: DSP noise subtraction
items: Speech and tones repeat; random noise does not
Autocorrelation: compares a signal with a delayed copy of itself
Adaptive filter: keeps adjusting itself to subtract the noise
DSP term for noise subtraction: adaptive filtering and autocorrelation
Noise blanking and limiting only suppress impulse noise peaks

onScreen: Blanking and limiting: impulse peaks only
scenes.narration: How can DSP tell noise from a voice? Speech and tones have patterns that repeat from moment to moment, while random noise never repeats. Autocorrelation compares the signal with a slightly delayed copy of itself, so whatever repeats stands out, and whatever doesn't must be noise. An adaptive filter is a filter that keeps adjusting itself, over and over, to subtract that noise. So the digital signal processing term for noise subtraction circuitry is adaptive filtering and autocorrelation. Noise blanking and noise limiting are different, simpler tools: they only suppress sharp impulse noise peaks, like clicks from an engine. In short, DSP cleans up audio by keeping what repeats and subtracting what doesn't.

callouts.label: Block 4: the AGC circuit, fed from the detector
Its DC voltage rises with signal strength
A DC voltmeter at point 4 monitors signal strength

onScreen: DC voltage rises with signal strength
DC voltmeter at point 4: signal strength
scenes.narration: Our last topic is receiver performance: keeping the receiver steady and clean. Start with the AGC, block 4 in pool Figure 3F15. Signals fade in and out, and stations differ hugely in strength. The AGC takes a sample from the detector and turns it into a DC, or direct current, voltage: a steady voltage that doesn't swing back and forth. The stronger the signal, the higher that voltage. Fed back to the IF amplifiers, it turns their gain down for strong signals and up for weak ones. Because it rises with signal strength, a DC voltmeter, a meter that measures voltage, connected at point 4 can monitor signal strength. Points 1, 2 and 3 are the mixer, oscillator and detector.

params.title: Where low-pass filters belong
items: AVC: automatic volume control, another name for AGC
AVC circuit: a low-pass filter smooths the detected signal into steady DC
Power supply: a low-pass filter removes ripple
Oscillator stage: not normally a low-pass filter

onScreen: Low-pass filter in the AVC circuit
Low-pass filter in the power supply
scenes.narration: That AGC voltage must be steady, which takes a filter. The same circuit is also called AVC, automatic volume control. The detector's output still carries the audio, which changes quickly. A low-pass filter in the AVC circuit lets only the slow changes through, smoothing it into a steady DC control voltage that follows signal strength, not every syllable. The power supply needs one too. It turns the AC supply into DC, and a low-pass filter removes the leftover ripple, a small wobble that would otherwise cause hum. The oscillator stage generates RF, so a low-pass filter isn't a normal part of it. So you find low-pass filters in the AVC circuit and the power supply, but not the oscillator.

params.title: Cross-modulation or intermodulation?
rows: A strong station's modulation on top of yours

onScreen: Unwanted modulation heard with the desired signal
Intermodulation: new signals on new frequencies
scenes.narration: Even with good AGC, a very strong station nearby can cause trouble. In cross-modulation, a strong unwanted signal drives a receiver stage harder than it can handle, and its modulation gets pressed onto the signal you're listening to. Cross-modulation interference is the term for signals from a very strong station superimposed on other signals being received. Put another way, it's modulation from an unwanted signal heard in addition to the desired signal: you hear your station, with the other station's voice riding on top. Intermodulation, by contrast, creates new signals on new frequencies, as we saw earlier.

params.title: Ignition noise and ferrite beads
items: Every spark: a sharp burst of radio noise
Ferrite bead: a magnetic ceramic ring that soaks up RF on a wire
Install them in the primary and secondary ignition leads

onScreen: Every spark: a burst of radio noise
scenes.narration: Not all interference comes from other stations. Some is made right beside the radio, by engines. Each time a spark plug fires, the spark is a sudden jolt of current, and that sends out a burst of radio noise across many frequencies. The wiring carries it and radiates it like a little antenna. A ferrite bead is a small ring of magnetic ceramic slipped over a wire. It barely affects steady current, but it soaks up high-frequency energy and turns it into a little heat. To suppress ignition noise, install ferrite beads in the primary and secondary ignition leads. The primary is the low-voltage wiring to the ignition coil; the secondary is the high-voltage side that feeds the plugs.

params.title: Noise that follows engine speed
items: Popping that rises and falls with engine speed: spark plug pulses
Fix: resistances in series with the spark plug wires
Resistance damps the current spikes, so less noise radiates

onScreen: Resistances in series with spark plug wires
scenes.narration: Spark noise has a telltale sound: in a car radio, it's a popping that speeds up and slows down with the engine. That's the clue: it comes from the spark plugs, firing faster as the engine revs. Pulse type interference to automobile radio receivers that appears related to the speed of the engine can often be reduced by installing resistances in series with the spark plug wires. The added resistance damps the sudden current spikes, and gentler current radiates less noise. That's why cars use resistor plugs or resistor wire. Heavy battery cables, or grounding the battery, won't touch noise made at the plugs.

params.title: Key facts to remember
items: RF stage: sets the noise figure and rejects the image; IF stages give most gain
IF just wider than the signal: FM 15, AM 10, SSB voice 2.4 kHz
Filters: Butterworth flat, Chebyshev ripple, m-derived trap near cut-off
Detectors: diode for AM, product for SSB and CW, discriminator for FM
Squelch: noise, CTCSS tones or DCS codes; AGC voltage shows signal strength

onScreen: RF stage: noise figure and image; IF: gain
Squelch: noise, tones, codes; AGC voltage
scenes.narration: To wrap up, 5 things to remember. First, the RF stage sets the noise figure and rejects the image, which sits the same IF distance on the far side of the LO. The IF stages give most of the gain. Second, make the IF filter slightly wider than the signal: 15 kilohertz for wideband FM, 10 for double-sideband AM, and 2.4 for SSB voice. Third, filters: a Butterworth is maximally flat, a Chebyshev allows ripple, and an m-derived filter adds a trap just past the cut-off. Fourth, detectors: a diode for AM, a product detector for SSB and CW, a discriminator for FM. Fifth, squelch works on noise, tones or codes, and the AGC voltage rises with signal strength.
